articles.title: A doctor, four clubs, and a beginning
articles.intro: Dr W. M. Brown brought an enthusiasm for golf to Tauranga. Within a year of his arrival, a club was taking shape.
paragraphs: Brown arrived from Dunedin in 1903. The book identifies a Bay of Plenty Times report of 20 April 1904 as the earliest written evidence of a golf club being formed in Tauranga. That distinction matters: 1903 begins this collection, while 1904 is the foundation year supported by the book.

By May 1905, the newspaper was reporting Brown’s re-election as captain and J. Bull’s re-election as secretary. The re-elections are another indication that this was already an established organisation.

The history recalls Brown arriving in a two-wheel gig driven by Arthur Faulkner. His bag held just four hickory-shafted clubs: a driver/brassie, cleek, lofter and putter. Ossie Daines carried them for sixpence. These details come from recollections assembled in the book, rather than surviving club minutes.
In June 1906, members of the golf and other local clubs joined a farewell dinner for Brown at the Masonic Hotel. His stay was short, but the game he helped establish endured.

articles.title: Golf between the Domain and the sea
articles.intro: Rugby players, tidal water and grazing animals were part of the challenge on Tauranga’s first course.
paragraphs: The early course began at Wharepai Domain and extended below The Elms towards Sulphur Point. The book describes a route through shared recreation grounds and low-lying coastal land, with a tin shed serving as a clubhouse.
One hole crossed the rugby ground. Another led to a green surrounded by water at high tide, reached by stepping-stones. The hazards were inseparable from the landscape and its other uses.

A surviving course card reproduced in the book records nine holes totalling 1,860 yards, with a bogey rating of 38. The longest hole, The Camp, measured 420 yards. Bogey was then used in the sense now associated with par.

The card is useful evidence, but its exact date is unresolved. Mowat notes that one hole is named Anzac, which raises a question about how that name fits the card’s presumed early date. It should not be treated as an independently dated 1904 document.

Conditions also changed over time: the 1908 meeting report describes a competition requiring two rounds of an eight-hole course. The book speculates about the missing hole; this preview leaves the reason open.

articles.title: A new home at Gate Pa
articles.intro: The move to the Racecourse Reserve gave the club room to grow, but making a course took the work of its members.
paragraphs: The foreword places the first approaches to the Racecourse Reserve trustees in 1913. In 1914, the club took up a lease at the reserve and moved away from the increasingly crowded Domain grounds.

The land was exposed and initially unpromising. Members cleared gorse, protected greens with fences, built stiles and prepared the ground. Auckland professional Fred Rutter was engaged to lay out eighteen holes, including holes inside the racecourse oval.

The first lease was for seven years. That offered a home for golf without the long-term security the club would later obtain. The course became known as Gate Pa, although the book points out that the reserve is in Greerton.

A transport notice reproduced on page 27, dated 20 June 1914, arranged Saturday cars from the corner of Wharf Street and The Strand. Players had to tell the secretary by Friday night if they wanted a seat.

The photograph reproduced with that notice shows The Avenue, the original first hole (identified in the 2014 book as the eleventh). The photograph itself is not dated; its appearance alongside a 1914 notice does not establish when it was taken.

articles.title: Making a club from a tin shed
articles.date: Early Gate Pa years · dates not specified
articles.intro: Working bees, shared lunches and the seasonal rhythm of golf sustained the early club.
paragraphs: The book describes a corrugated iron shed shared with the racing club as the first clubhouse at the reserve. A long table and forms occupied most of the room; primus stoves and kettles supplied tea.
Members brought paper-wrapped lunches, and many cycled to the course with clubs on their backs. A cookhouse and stove came later, although the passage does not give a precise year for the change.

Golf was largely a winter activity. In summer, the fairways produced hay; greens were prepared for a new season in March. Grazing animals and an occasional horse-drawn mower helped maintain the playing areas.
The women’s committee catered for visiting players under difficult conditions. Mowat records meals prepared at home and brought to the club, alongside the work of cleaning and preparing the shed.

These passages describe the early Gate Pa years broadly. They are included as context, rather than assigned to a particular year between 1914 and 1923. The accompanying golfing-party photograph is also undated and is not identified as a view of this shed.

articles.title: Names on the early honours boards
articles.intro: The championship lists preserve a dated thread through years for which other records are incomplete.
paragraphs: A. Matheson won the men’s senior championship in 1911 and 1912, and again in 1921. The introduction explains how the honours boards beginning in 1911 helped that year become accepted for a time as the club’s foundation date. The later research presented in the book instead supports 1904.

The men’s list records H. Phillips in 1913, no championship played in 1914, J. Fowles in 1915 and 1916, R. Renshaw in 1917, H. J. Rowe in 1918, and R. H. Roache in 1919. It gives Renshaw again in 1920, 1922 and 1923. The list does not explain why the 1914 championship was not played.

The women’s senior championship list begins in 1919 with Mrs G. Henderson. Miss R. Daines won in 1920, 1921 and 1922; Miss N. Wallis is listed for 1923. A separate biographical passage identifies the three-time winner as Rennie Daines.
The women’s list starting in 1919 should not be read as evidence that women only began playing then: the book names women members and mixed competition much earlier.
These names close the collection’s first chapter in 1923. Later chapters follow the playing record through the decades, with the full honours lists retained in the book’s appendices.

articles.title: A club finding its stride
articles.intro: Photographs and championship records show a growing club before the major changes of the 1930s.
paragraphs: The championship lists offer one way into the interwar years. The men’s senior title went to G. Pott in 1924 and 1926, R. P. Baigent in 1925 and A. Matheson in 1927. The women’s list records Mrs D. V. Hanna in 1924 and 1926, Mrs R. Burke in 1925 and Miss C. Humphreys in 1927.

The book’s profile of Elsie Hanna says she arrived in Tauranga in 1922 and served on the Ladies’ committee from 1926 to 1939. Such service is another part of the record alongside the championship results.

A photograph of closing day in 1931 gathers members outside the jockey’s room, which served as the early clubhouse. Other photographs identify Connie Humphreys in 1927 and a group at lunch in 1932. They give faces and everyday settings to an otherwise sparse written record.

The course still included holes within the racecourse oval. An old scorecard reproduced on page 29 records that earlier layout; the book describes a substantial redesign in 1934. These images and records provide a bridge from the first Gate Pa years to the next phase of development.

articles.title: Beyond the racecourse oval
articles.intro: A redesign helped transform the early Gate Pa layout into a more settled golf course.
paragraphs: The original Gate Pa course extended into the racecourse oval. In its account of 1934, the book describes the club commissioning Auckland professional Alex Murray to advise on a new layout.

The review removed the five holes using the oval and changed other parts of the route. Members had also hoped to avoid the demanding climbs associated with The Drop and The Hummocks. Retained holes were renumbered around the new sequence.

The account links this change with a growing determination to move beyond makeshift playing conditions. References to present-day hole numbers in the book describe the course as it stood in 2014; they should not be assumed to describe every later alteration.

One date needs care: page 37 associates the 1934 changes with a new 33-year lease, while page 23 places the board’s authority to grant that lease term in 1944. This preview retains the stated redesign date but does not use the disputed lease detail to explain it. The original lease and course records would help settle that point.

articles.title: Professional help, a new chapter
articles.intro: James Mowat and experienced greenkeeper W. H. Coles arrived as the club sought better golf and better playing conditions.
paragraphs: The history reproduces a Bay of Plenty Times report dated 30 March 1936 announcing two appointments: W. H. Coles as greenkeeper and James Mowat as the club’s professional.

Coles had worked at Napier Golf Club. Mowat came from Poverty Bay with experience in Scotland and the United States. The report presented their skills as an opportunity to improve both the course and the standard of play.

Tuition mattered for beginners and established golfers alike. The report emphasised the value of learning sound habits early and having someone able to identify faults in a more experienced player’s swing.

James was Dave Mowat’s father. The book’s introduction acknowledges that family connection, and its later account recalls James supporting junior golfers’ right to enter club championships during the 1950s. His contribution ran beyond the professional appointment itself.

articles.title: A clubhouse of their own
articles.intro: The shared tin shed gave way to a dedicated clubhouse, a milestone recorded in photographs.
paragraphs: The first Gate Pa clubhouse was a corrugated iron building shared with racing. The history describes crowded seating, shared lunches and the small comforts members gradually added to it.
In 1938 a dedicated clubhouse was built on the area the 2014 book identifies as the car park. Photographs record its opening and show Miss Eva Goodyear beside the trophies.

Two further views show the wooden building and the open ground around it. The building date is known, but those views are not individually dated. They show the clubhouse built in 1938 without establishing that each photograph was taken that year.

After the war the building could no longer comfortably serve the enlarged membership. When a new clubhouse opened in 1954, the old wooden structure was sold and moved to Pyes Pa, where the book says it became a home again.

articles.title: Nine holes and a different purpose
articles.intro: During the Second World War, part of the course was put to food production while a smaller course remained in play.
paragraphs: The book describes the course being reduced to nine holes during the war. The eighth, ninth and tenth fairways were ploughed and planted with potatoes, while other areas were left to grow hay.
Greenkeeper Mr Reeves maintained the remaining nine holes with limited equipment. The racecourse and its buildings also served as headquarters for the National Reserve, with members training there.

The Ladies’ minutes summarised in the history record fundraising for the Patriotic Shop in 1940. These contributions place the club within the wider demands of wartime, beyond the reduced playing programme.

The men’s senior championship appendix records no competition from 1941 to 1945. Accounts of the women’s wartime championships vary within the book: the appendix lists Anne Mark in 1941, while her profile describes that year as a gap. That discrepancy remains open for checking rather than being silently resolved.

articles.title: A course restored, a membership growing
articles.intro: Returning players and increasing membership brought new energy—and new demands on the club.
paragraphs: After the war, members worked to restore the full eighteen-hole course. The history associates that effort with returning servicemen and women eager to resume peacetime pursuits.
By 1951 the book records 416 members, an unprecedented total for the club. The wooden clubhouse that had opened in 1938 was becoming too small for the number of people using it.
The next phase included plans for a new building and continued improvement in course care. Grant Silvester took over as head greenkeeper in 1951, beginning a long association with the course.

This was more than a recovery of the prewar routine. It set up the clubhouse project, the Veterans’ Society and the expanded tournament programme that would make the 1950s such an active decade. The accompanying image shows the clubhouse built in 1954, after this period of growth.
Access improved as well: the book records sealing the first section of the entrance road in 1958, with the remaining section completed in 1960. The latter improvement falls just beyond this chapter.

articles.title: Building for a bigger club
articles.intro: Members helped finance a new clubhouse as postwar growth outstripped the old building.
paragraphs: The history records the sale of four hundred £10 debentures to help finance a new brick clubhouse. Alan Davidson, Dave Cambie and Lionel Smith formed the building committee.
The new building opened in 1954, on the site used by the later clubhouse. Photographs on page 55 show two views of the building, with the putting area and open course beside it.

The old wooden clubhouse was sold and relocated to Pyes Pa. The choice of the new building’s position had prompted debate, a reminder that even a widely welcomed improvement could raise different views among members.

The financial figures need verification: page 53 describes a construction ceiling of £5,700 and completion below budget; the later committee summary gives a cost of £5,750. Those passages may use different cost bases, but the book does not settle that question. The debenture record and opening year are presented separately from the unresolved final cost.

articles.title: The work behind the Wednesday game
articles.intro: Committee records show women shaping competition, fundraising and opportunities to play.
paragraphs: The book’s extracts from the Ladies’ minutes record a 1937 discussion about separating the men’s and ladies’ sections. The proposal was not adopted at that time. Later entries show the women organising competitions and undertaking essential work around the clubhouse.

In 1946 businesswomen asked to play their competitions on Saturday afternoons. The source records the request without giving the response. It is a small but telling example of how access to playing time mattered.

The 1952 minutes describe a Ways and Means Committee for the building programme. In 1953, the committee resolved that competition results and club news should be published in the Bay of Plenty Times; in 1954, a vote established Wednesday as club day.

Dr Jean Reading introduced a competition for school-age girls in 1955. The following year the minutes recorded insufficient interest to continue it. This short-lived initiative belongs in the junior story as well as the women’s record: encouragement did not always produce an enduring programme on its first attempt.

articles.title: Anne Mark: playing and making things happen
articles.intro: A player and administrator whose contribution reached well beyond her own competitions.
paragraphs: Anne Mark joined the club in 1935. Her recollections include helping Elsie Hanna prepare catering by gathering kindling and cutting firewood for the racing club’s range.
She first served as handicap manager in 1938 and held several positions on the Ladies’ committee. Her account in the book describes a practical involvement in the daily work that kept the club going.

Anne also assisted the Veterans’ Society with its first five-day tournament in 1953, working alongside Rennie Gordon, later Wallis. The Veterans’ history credits the two women with the clerical organisation behind those early tournaments.

In her account, Anne places the formation of the Bay of Plenty Ladies’ Golf Association in 1954 and records serving as its president for three years. She joined the national Ladies’ Golf Union council in 1955. Those roles connect the local club’s story to the wider administration of women’s golf.

articles.title: Una Wickham and the wider golfing world
articles.intro: A Tauranga player whose achievements connected the club to provincial and national golf.
paragraphs: Una Wickham joined Tauranga Golf Club in 1954 and represented Bay of Plenty in the Russell Grace interprovincial tournament that year. The team won, with further wins recorded in 1955 and 1959.

The book describes Una’s earlier international experience and her interest in more demanding playing conditions for leading women. It also records resistance to her choice of slacks in cold weather, illustrating the conventions women competitors faced.
At club level she began a run of seven consecutive senior championship wins in 1954. The appendix lists her as champion in every year from 1954 through 1959, the end of this chapter’s coverage.

In 1959 she won the New Zealand amateur championship, an achievement identified both in her profile and beside her portrait. Her later record extends well beyond the 1950s and will be developed in a future chapter. The portrait itself is undated; the caption lists titles rather than fixing when the photograph was taken.

articles.title: The beginnings of the Veterans’ Society
articles.intro: Friendly rounds grew into an organised society and an ambitious annual tournament.
paragraphs: The Veterans’ history traces the group’s origins to informal games after the Second World War. In 1952 it became an organised association, with John McKenzie as president and Dick Phelan as secretary.

In November 1953, a group of just 23 members staged a five-day tournament. Anne Mark and Rennie Gordon assisted with the organisation, and the event established a pattern that would continue for many years.

The group adopted the name Veterans’ Society in the mid-1950s to distinguish itself from the national association. In 1955 its summer programme included the Angus Plate, donated by Gavin Wallace. Veterans’ day changed to Thursday in 1957.

Tauranga hosted the national veterans’ championship in 1959. E. S. Toogood of Poverty Bay won, with Tauranga’s Frank Macklow runner-up. These events give the Senior Men collection an early foundation; later service projects and present-day activities can be added as separate records.

Much of this section of the book reproduces a 1977 history compiled by Bill Sanders and Ken McIntyre. The main narrative dates the first five-day tournament to 1953; a later passage mentions a 1951 tournament. This preview follows the explicit 1953 account and leaves the inconsistent reference noted for review.

articles.title: Inviting New Zealand to Tauranga
articles.intro: A national invitation tournament helped show the course to players and spectators beyond the district.
paragraphs: The 1952–53 committee wanted to attract visiting golfers and new members. Working with the New Zealand PGA, it planned a 54-hole invitation tournament for June 1953.

The first field included eighteen professionals and forty-two invited amateurs. Frank Buckler led the professionals with 216, four ahead of Alex Murray. Tori Jones of Taumarunui headed the amateur field by one stroke.

The event returned through the decade. The book records a round of 64 by Alex Murray in 1954, another win for Buckler in 1955, and a commanding performance by amateur Stuart Jones in 1956. Local professional Jimmy Paterson won the professional division that year.

The ambition was both to promote the course and to let younger players see leading golfers in action. The illustrated Labour Weekend group, dated approximately 1950, belongs to the wider tournament culture at the club; it is not a photograph of the 1953 invitation event.

articles.title: Opening the way for younger players
articles.intro: The book recalls a debate over schoolboys’ championship eligibility and an early competition for schoolgirls.
paragraphs: Dave Mowat records that Michael Cambie and Robert Mowat qualified for club championships during the 1950s but encountered objections because they were schoolboys paying junior subscriptions.

James Mowat and others supported their right to compete. According to the account, those arguments prevailed and the boys were allowed to participate. The recollection does not give an exact year, so this story remains dated to the decade.

The Ladies’ minutes record a different attempt to encourage younger players: Dr Jean Reading’s 1955 competition for school-age girls. It did not continue the following year because there was insufficient interest.

The photograph of Labour Weekend contenders around 1950 includes a barefoot caddie identified in the book as Brian Ducker. It shows another way younger people encountered the game. The boy in that image is not identified as either of the championship players discussed here.

articles.title: A shorter round, a wider welcome
articles.intro: Tauranga played a pioneering role in nine-hole golf, with Phyll Sandlant helping turn an invitation to try the game into a substantial club group.
paragraphs: The book describes a 1977 move to provide nine-hole handicaps for women who found a full round difficult. It presents that local provision as a forerunner of the later organised movement.

In Phyll Sandlant’s account reproduced by Mowat, an advertisement in February 1998 invited women to try nine-hole golf at Tauranga. Ninety-six women registered. Professional Rick Barker provided coaching, with volunteers accompanying beginners and introducing the game’s etiquette and competition formats.

The inaugural BOPTV Honda Nine Hole Tournament followed at Tauranga in 1999. The book credits Phyll and the volunteers who supported her, as well as Alison Holdem and Lynn Goodhew who carried the work forward. Phyll became a life member in 2006.

A separate 2014 centenary report in SunLive identifies Patsy Hankins as instrumental in the national initiative and says she approached Phyll in 1998 to help implement it. That report calls Tauranga the first New Zealand club; Phyll’s account in the book specifically describes the first group in Bay of Plenty. Both sources show Tauranga’s pioneering contribution, while describing the scope differently.

The Ladies 9 Hole collection links this history to the club group’s own records. Present-day membership, programmes and achievements can be added as new, dated contributions rather than assumed from the 2014 account.

external_sources.title: Luke Balvert, “A hole in 100”, SunLive, 15 November 2014

articles.title: Subtle changes, a lasting influence
articles.intro: John Harris’s advice helped shape the course without turning it into something its members would no longer recognise.
paragraphs: In 1967 the club invited British golf architect Commander John Harris to inspect the course. His report described changes intended to improve a club course rather than force it into the mould of a long championship layout.

Greens chairman Alan Davidson and superintendent Grant Silvester walked the course with Harris. The book describes Davidson preparing models from the advice and Silvester and his team putting the proposals into practice, with help from Garth Renner.
The changes concentrated on lines of play, bunkering and mounding. Dave’s account values their subtlety and the variety offered by the existing ground.

The original chapter also carries a hole-by-hole history and later reflections on design. Those passages remain available in the book collection, rather than being compressed into a single date on the timeline.

articles.title: Water: the work beneath the fairways
articles.intro: A reliable water supply took decades of investigation, investment and practical adjustment.
paragraphs: The earliest system drew from the Borough supply, with sprinklers that needed shifting by hand. Some greens were beyond the pipe network, and water pressure depended on demands elsewhere in the town.
The book records investigating the nearby stream in 1963 and a bore in 1970. A reservoir and further pipework followed, but keeping enough water available remained a difficulty.
In 1978 the club approved a more extensive reticulation system. By the 1990s its limitations had prompted another major decision: a professionally designed replacement, completed in April 1995.

The chapter explains both the engineering and the work of staff who moved sprinklers, often at night. Its technical descriptions and water-right references describe the position when the book was written, not current operating instructions.

A related change was the gradual conversion of fairways to Windsor Green, reducing the need for summer watering. The separate Windsor Green story follows the book’s planting history and the later club-history account of the supplier arrangement and the use of the club’s own resources.

articles.title: A landscape planted by people
articles.intro: Trees gave shelter and shape to the course, and many also carried personal memories.
paragraphs: Dave traces a major planting programme to A. J. Mirrielees and the relief-worker scheme during the Depression. Later members continued the work, adding both useful shelter and individual specimen trees.

The chapter records the history of particular trees, their loss in storms, and the debate that often accompanied removal or replacement. It presents planting as part of course design as well as beautification.
It also considers how species selection affects turf, maintenance and wildlife. These observations are Dave’s account and opinions, preserved in the original chapter with its date and context.
The stories of planting and care belong alongside the playing records: the landscape experienced by each generation was partly the result of work by the people before it.

articles.title: Women at the committee table
articles.intro: From Nen Sim’s election to a woman president, representation changed the club’s leadership.
paragraphs: Evelyn, known as Nen, Sim became the first woman elected to the club executive in 1974. The book describes her practical contribution and her concern for the interests of the whole membership.
A 1978 decision provided for a woman appointed from the women’s section as well as those elected directly. Loeta Hutcheson and Peg Cross were among those who followed that route.
When the Board structure arrived in 1994, women again took part in its development. Dave’s account records Joyce Paris among the first elected Board members and Noeline Shiel as vice president.

Peg Copestake became club president in 2000, the first woman to hold that office. The original administration chapter follows the transition in greater detail, including the discussions about responsibilities and representation.

articles.title: A new way to run the club
articles.intro: The move from a general committee to a Board introduced new responsibilities and a period of adjustment.
paragraphs: The new Board structure took effect in 1994. The first elected members were Bruce Partridge and Joyce Paris, joined by president Noel Copestake and players’ representative Paul Munn; Ian Cross and Jackie McDonald were invited to fill the remaining positions.

Bruce Partridge served as inaugural chair. The book describes the early work of defining the roles of Board, general manager and players’ committees, alongside different views about the new arrangements.
Later Boards worked on finance, course improvement and the clubhouse. Dave gives particular attention to the planning behind the redevelopment and to leadership documents prepared by Grant Scoones.
This is the book’s account of the transition, including its author’s assessments. The full administration chapter preserves the detail and names so members can read beyond this short introduction.

articles.title: The clubhouse rebuilt for a new century
articles.intro: Planning, member expertise and a major financial commitment produced the clubhouse that opened in April 2001.
paragraphs: In February 1999 the Board established a Facilities Advisory Group to examine the clubhouse. Its members brought experience in construction, drafting, engineering, management and cost estimation.

The proposal used the existing foundations and basement rather than building elsewhere on the course. A July 2000 meeting considered the options and financing, including funds made available when the Golf Club Trust was wound up.

During the work, club life continued in temporary accommodation. The book acknowledges caterers Peter and Tania Robb, bar staff and professional Rick Barker for keeping services going through the disruption.
The new facility opened with a champagne breakfast in April 2001. Dave credits both the formal planning and the members who gave their expertise to bring the project to completion.

articles.title: The women veterans find their own rhythm
articles.intro: Monthly golf, visits and shared lunches built another enduring part of club life.
paragraphs: The book traces the women veterans’ group to the initiative of Jean Mack and Phyl Carter in 1987. At the first formal annual meeting in November 1988, Marg Calver was elected president.

Competition was only part of the attraction. Bus trips, lunches, visits with other clubs and Christmas gatherings helped establish the group’s character. Members also supported improvements to club facilities.
Nine-hole players joined the monthly competitions by 1999. The chapter records how the programme adapted as both nine-hole and eighteen-hole membership grew.

The original chapter retains the names of organisers and the sequence of events through the period covered by the book. It gives this group a clear place within the Ladies collection without assuming that its 2014 programme describes today’s arrangements.

articles.title: The projects behind the pleasure
articles.intro: The Veterans’ contribution extended from friendly rounds to practical work around the course.
paragraphs: In 1985 the Veterans proposed undertaking projects agreed with the club in return for relief from course fees for their annual tournament. The book records the arrangement and lists the work carried out in the years that followed.

Projects ranged from painting, paths and ball washers to gardens, steps, signs and improvements to tees and greens. The year-by-year record shows how many small jobs accumulated into a substantial contribution.
The account also recognises the volunteers who maintained the Society’s album and the group associated with firewood and tree work. These were contributions in time and skill as well as in money.

The original Veterans’ chapter includes the full project lists, office holders and personalities. New Senior Men records can continue that pattern, while keeping the book’s historical account distinct from current activities.

articles.title: When the day’s work was done
articles.intro: Twilight golf brought together summer evenings, volunteers and a different route into the club.
paragraphs: Twilight tournaments began in the summer of 1974–75. The events used ten holes because the tenth finished near the clubhouse, making a shared meal a natural part of the evening.

Nen Sim and a team of volunteers organised early catering and kept careful records. Later, Noel Copestake and others developed a programme able to handle much larger fields, with several starting routes and their own cards.

Business House golf grew under Gary Baker’s encouragement, bringing teams and players without club membership into the evening competition. The chapter describes both its social appeal and its logistical demands.

Dave also records the development of a twilight handicap system and its eventual incorporation into the club’s computer software. The system described is historical; current conditions of competition belong on the operational club website.

articles.title: The people behind the professional’s counter
articles.intro: Teaching, equipment, encouragement and the running of a business all formed part of the professional’s role.
paragraphs: The book follows the resident professionals from James Mowat to Jim Paterson, Greg Holst, Allan Snape, Rick Barker and the later shop team. Each worked with the facilities and circumstances of a different period.
Jim Paterson’s teaching style and ball striking receive close attention. Later profiles describe professional experience, business changes and the personal relationships that developed with members.

The 1986 fire in the shop and trundler shed was a major interruption during Allan Snape’s time. The account records the loss of stock and members’ equipment and the club’s response to help the family.

Rick Barker’s work with beginners connects directly to the development of nine-hole golf. Jay Carter’s story connects junior golf, professional training and the continuing service of the shop. All the profiles can be read in their original chapter.

articles.title: Making good golf possible
articles.intro: Behind every round lay the work of the greenkeepers and the changing science of turf care.
paragraphs: Grant Silvester took charge in 1951. The book describes his long service and the practical care involved in maintaining the course with the machinery, water supply and knowledge then available.

Later staff worked through changes in turf management and expectations. Dave’s account includes Grant Patterson, Murray Clark and Graeme Reinders, among others, and distinguishes periods of repair, improvement and new construction.

The chapter considers grass species, greens, bunkers, machinery and the effect of local conditions. It also acknowledges the staff teams and volunteers whose work could be less visible than a new building or a tournament result.
Its technical observations belong to the time of writing. Preserving the chapter lets readers see how course care developed without treating a 2014 description as today’s maintenance policy.

articles.title: From record books to card readers
articles.intro: Handicapping became a less visible but increasingly technical part of keeping competition fair.
paragraphs: The book contrasts early discretionary systems with the record-keeping required after the national adoption of a USGA-based system for men in 1962. Arnold Shanks maintained large quantities of cards and handwritten records alongside his other club duties.
Dave discusses the move to Slope in September 2000 and the practical task of comparing performance across courses. These passages reflect the rules and systems then in use.
The chapter also records an early computer demonstration by Tauranga Boys’ College staff and students and, later, approval of Golf Autoscore in 2005.

It is a history of how the club managed the task, not a guide to the current handicap system. The full chapter preserves the examples, disagreements and personal recollections that give the subject its local character.

articles.title: In the members’ own voices
articles.intro: Arnold Shanks and other members describe the people, rounds and incidents that official records rarely capture.
paragraphs: The personal-experiences chapter begins with Arnold Shanks, who served as steward and bar manager from 1967 to 1983. His recollections connect farming life, Saturday golf and the everyday hospitality of the club.

Other accounts describe learning the game, caddying, competition, family connections and memorable incidents. Their value lies partly in the different vantage points from which members remembered the same place.
These are attributed recollections, rather than a single independently verified chronology. Where the book signals uncertainty or an approximate date, the website retains that context.

The full chapter is available in the book collection, page by page, with its names and original wording. Search the collection for a person or follow the chapter’s story headings to find a particular account.

articles.title: A family woven into club life
articles.intro: The Ward family story spans championship golf, committee work and the next generation.
paragraphs: Fred Ward’s arrival in 1947 began a long family association with Tauranga Golf Club. His championship and open-tournament record made him a central figure in the postwar playing story.
His brothers Allen and Claude, widely known as Buster, later joined the club. The chapter follows their playing careers and the wider contributions of the family.
John Ward joined as a junior in 1967 and went on to provincial representative golf and club titles. Errol’s involvement included service as club captain around the turn of the century.

The original family chapter gives the relationships, results and memories in fuller form. It provides a model for later family contributions: a connected account with named people and sources, rather than isolated names on an honours board.

articles.title: The stars come to Gate Pa
articles.intro: The Spalding Masters brought international visitors, large galleries and remarkable scoring to the course.
paragraphs: The book records the Spalding approach in 1967 and the first tournament in January 1968. The event gave Tauranga a place on the growing summer circuit.
Billy Dunk won the inaugural event, while scoring and course-record debates became part of the story. In 1969 Bob Charles produced a total of 260, with rounds that included 62 and 63.

The chapter follows the changing fields and contests over successive years, including Stuart Jones’s challenge to the professionals. It records the spectators and atmosphere as well as the winning totals.
The original year-by-year account continues into the NZPGA events staged at Tauranga. Its details can be explored by page, keeping the short overview separate from the full tournament narrative.

articles.title: National championship days
articles.intro: Tauranga’s NZPGA championships brought leading professionals back to the club.
paragraphs: Tauranga first staged the NZPGA championship in January 1974 after the Mount Maunganui greens required rebuilding. The book explains that connection before turning to the tournament itself.
The later accounts include a dramatic 1977 finish between John Lister and Allan Brask. Lister drew level late and won the play-off, with spectators crowding around the closing holes.
In 1978 Simon Owen emerged as winner after Guy Wolstenholme lost ground at the finish. The 1980 account returns to Bob Charles and the pressure of tournament putting.
These are fuller stories than a list of champions can convey. The original chapter retains the rounds, turning points, comments and local connections for readers who want to follow them.

articles.title: A match worth watching
articles.intro: Exhibition matches let members watch leading golfers in a different setting from a full tournament.
paragraphs: The book records Kel Nagle playing Jim Paterson in 1960, the match finishing all square. A year later Bob Charles played the local professional and won two and one.
Another account recalls Peter Thomson playing Fred Ward, including a difficult lie under the boundary hedge. The interest lies as much in the incident and the response as in the outcome.
The chapter shows how the club tried to bring high-quality golf to its members, even when the economics of a single match were modest.
The full exhibition chapter carries the remaining visitors, recollections and details, with the original page references preserved.

articles.title: Professional golf returns
articles.intro: The Carrus Tauranga Open introduced another generation of leading players to the club.
paragraphs: The book describes the club joining a series promoted by Greg Turner, with Paul and Sheryl Adams of Carrus Corporation becoming the name sponsors. The first tournament in this account was held in 2006.
Local amateur Josh Geary won that first event. Dave’s account follows his contest with Kevin Smith and the recovery from a difficult hole in the third round.
Later tournaments brought further memorable performances. Richard Lee’s 59 in 2010 became a landmark round, while the 2011 event ended in a wet final-day battle won by Jim Cusdin.

The original chapter contains the year-by-year narratives, women’s results and local connections. Its coverage ends in 2011; later Carrus results can be added as new records without attributing them to the book.

articles.title: Remembering Una through competition
articles.intro: The women’s match-play tournament became a memorial to a player who had inspired the club.
paragraphs: The book follows the women’s open match-play tournament from its first staging in 1976. After Una Wickham’s death in 1983, the women’s committee developed the event in her memory.

Its fields drew leading players from across the northern regions and, for a time, provided a useful test for interprovincial selectors. The year-by-year account names finalists, winners and close matches.
Dave also reflects on the later difficulty of sustaining the event’s profile as players’ priorities and programmes changed.

The original tournament chapter preserves the detail behind the memorial. It connects naturally with Una’s profile and the wider women’s collection, while keeping the tournament’s origins distinct from the later memorial name.

articles.title: A new place to learn and practise
articles.intro: The short-course facility opened another way into the game at the end of the period covered by the book.
paragraphs: The final chapter begins with a concrete development: a short-course and practice facility on land beside the second fairway. The book credits legal and planning work that made use of the area possible.

Club champion Dave Cooke and professional Jay Carter designed a flexible layout for pitch-and-putt play, teaching and practice. Synthetic tees and greens were combined with Windsor Green fairways prepared by club staff.

The account acknowledges a Lion Foundation grant arranged through Michelle Towersey and Chris McAlpine. It describes the facility as an opportunity whose future use would depend on the people promoting and using it.

After this section, Dave turns to an imagined account of the next century. The website separates that imaginative ending from the historical timeline: predicted events in 2020 or later are not presented as facts.

articles.title: Making room for the next generation
articles.intro: Talent and encouragement gradually challenged the restrictions once placed on junior members.
paragraphs: The book includes memories of juniors being challenged over their right to compete or to use parts of the clubhouse. A later recollection describes Wayne Holden and Brent Sutherland playing extra holes in a senior championship match during the 1960s.

Another story recalls Michael Nicholson sitting with adult playing partners at a table placed across the boundary between the clubhouse’s carpet and linoleum, so he could comply with the rule excluding juniors from the lounge.

Against those restrictions stand the people who encouraged younger players, including Una Wickham, James Mowat and family members. The later profiles trace players such as Jay Carter through junior golf and into wider roles.

These memories are retained as accounts of the club’s changing culture. They offer a foundation for a Juniors collection that can also record today’s players, teams and opportunities in their own time.

articles.title: Dave looks a hundred years ahead
articles.intro: The book closes with a creative look forward, written as if a future historian were looking back.
paragraphs: Dave explicitly introduces the closing chapter as a prediction of how the club and course might develop over the next century. Much of it is written in the past tense from an imagined future viewpoint.
He considers climate, water, turf, equipment, course changes, the economy and the future appeal of golf. These passages reveal the concerns and hopes of the author at the time of writing.
They are not evidence that the predicted changes happened. The dates and developments described after the short-course section have therefore been excluded from the website’s historical timeline.
The full ending remains available as part of the book, labelled as an imagined future. Preserving that distinction honours the form Dave chose without turning his speculation into a historical claim.

articles.title: Windsor Green: changing the fairways, conserving water
articles.intro: Converting the fairways to Windsor Green changed how the club managed summer playing conditions and its demand for water.
paragraphs: The conversion to Windsor Green, a fine couch variety, became a significant part of Tauranga’s greenkeeping history. The Board’s approach combined improved summer playing conditions with reduced reliance on fairway watering. A club-history update supplied in November 2026 records the fairway conversion as almost complete and its contribution to reducing water use as substantial.

Mowat describes the choice facing the Board: install comprehensive fairway irrigation or establish grasses better able to withstand dry summers. David Ormsby advised the club on suitable Cynodon cultivars, with Windsor Green selected. The book records concerns about both the capital and continuing cost of irrigation and the long-term availability of enough water.

The Board at the time faced the prospect of replacing the club’s irrigation system at a substantial cost, potentially requiring significant debt. Avoiding the need to irrigate the fairways represented a major saving. The Board’s decision to pursue a grass that reduced reliance on fairway watering also showed foresight about water use, anticipating pressures that then lay well into the future.

Mowat places the first trial on the 11th and 13th fairways, with differing dates in the book: page 186 says 2000, while page 144 gives November 2001. The book remains the primary reference for the chronology; the precise trial date is retained as a source discrepancy.

The initial establishment was not straightforward. Mowat describes slow growth, members’ doubts and the need for staff to learn how to manage the new surface. Brendan Allen developed its management and proposed using material removed by grooving the established fairways to plant others. Windsor Green reduced the need for watering, but required mowing and mechanical treatment, and underwent winter dormancy.

The way the grass was obtained also helped make the conversion affordable. The later club-history account recalls an element of good fortune: the supplier placed no restriction on propagating the grass elsewhere on the course, avoiding what would ordinarily have been a separate cost for each fairway. The club could therefore manage its spread using existing staff, plant material and other club resources. This account of the supplier arrangement has not been checked against an original agreement.

The later book account supports the practical importance of propagation from within the course. Groovings were trialled on the second fairway and part of the sixth in 2005. Purchased turf was used for the rest of the sixth in 2006, but its cost and labour requirements encouraged a return to material taken from the club’s established fairways. Mowat records conversions of the eighth in 2008, the tenth in 2009 and the eighteenth in 2011.

This was also a story of staff and member effort. The veterans’ account on page 133 records volunteers laying Windsor Green stolons on the eighteenth fairway and in the turf nursery, placing that work in 2010; the water chapter dates the successful eighteenth-fairway conversion to 2011. The accounts may describe different stages of the work. The later short-course facility also used Windsor Green harvested from the established fairways, laid by club staff.

Taken together, the accounts describe a gradual change in the playing surface and in the club’s approach to water: establish suitable turf, learn how to manage it, and use material already growing on the course to extend the conversion. The November 2026 update records the programme as almost complete. This later information is separate from the book’s imagined future.
articles.source_note: Based on Pars from the Past, edited by David G. S. Mowat (2014), pp. 133, 143–146, 186–187 and 278–279, with a club-history update supplied in November 2026. The Board at the time is credited with the irrigation and water-use foresight. The supplier arrangement and near-completion by 2026 are later additions; no original supplier agreement or quantified water-use records have been supplied. Mowat’s account takes precedence for dates. The imagined future on pp. 280–284 has not been used as factual evidence.
